newsitem.title: USA: Sallie Mae wins decision on offset fee.
newsitem.headline: Sallie Mae wins decision on offset fee.

text.p: Student Loan Marketing Association (Sallie Mae) on Friday said the U.S. Department of Education decided that a 30 basis point offset fee did not apply to certain student loans securitized by Sallie Mae.
The offset fee is an annual fee that applied to guaranteed loans purchased by Sallie Mae from lenders.

As a result of Friday's decision, Sallie Mae will count as pretax income about $100 million that it had reserved in the event its legal challenge to the offset fee failed. Sallie Mae said the government's decision would have a favorable impact on earnings going forward.

"We have vigorously pursued this lawsuit, and we are delighted that the Department of Education supports our view that the offset fee does not apply to securitized loans," Timothy Greene, executive vice president and general counsel of Sallie Mae, said in a statement.

Sallie Mae sued in the U.S. District Court in Washington in April 1995, challenging the department's interpretation of a new law. In November 1995, the court ruled in favor of Sallie Mae, and its decision was later upheld by a federal appeals court.
Sallie Mae is a stockholder-owned, government-sponsored enterprise that buys loans from lenders and then sells them in the market through a process of securitization.

On July 31, Sallie Mae shareholders will vote on whether to privatize the company, ending the government tie, and also to elect one of two slates of directors. Sallie Mae management has proposed one slate and an opposition group, known as the Committee to Restore Value (CRV), has nominated another.
Greene said the legal effort was launched before the committee won board representation in 1995. The result shows that "management does not need the CRV to create value."
In April 1997, the district court ordered the Department of Education to take final action by July 31.

Sallie Mae released a copy of a letter from U.S. Secretary of Education Richard Riley informing it that the department determined that under the court rulings Sallie Mae's equity ownership in the securitized loans does not have a substantial value. "....We elect not to apply the fee to the loans under these circumstances," Riley said.
Riley said the decision could be different if Sallie Mae securitized loans and kept a greater equity interest.
